name: Addi
title: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
summary: Addi is a figure known exclusively from the genealogy in the Gospel of Luke, where he is placed as the son of Kosam and father of Melki. He belongs to the Davidic line that goes through David's son Nathan – unlike Matthew's genealogy, which follows the line through Solomon. Scripture gives no information about Addi's life, work, or character. Yet his place in the messianic lineage carries an important theological dimension: it testifies to God's faithful fulfillment of the covenant promises to David, as the line of promise is carried forward generation by generation until Jesus the Messiah.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus
keyEvents.description: Addi is listed as one of Jesus' ancestors in the genealogy that Luke presents. He is placed between his father Kosam and his son Melki in the line of generations from David to Jesus.

keyEvents.title: Part of Nathan's lineage
keyEvents.description: Addi belongs to the branch of David's descendants that goes through Nathan. Through this line, Luke shows that Jesus is a legitimate descendant of King David and that the messianic promises tied to David's family are fulfilled.

versions.summary: Addi is a person mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus in the Gospel of Luke. He is the son of Kosam and father of Melki, and is part of the lineage connecting David with Jesus through Nathan's line. Little is known about his life beyond his place in the messianic family line.
versions.title: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
versions.reason: [minor] Addi likely lived in the period between the exile and the time of Jesus. 'Return' (the return) is a reasonable placement, but 'intertestamental' could also be appropriate depending on the chronological position in the genealogy. Since there is great uncertainty about the exact time period, 'return' is acceptable.; [minor] The role 'patriarch' is usually used for the great forefathers (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, etc.). For an unknown person in a genealogy, 'ancestor of Jesus' or 'forefather' would be more precise. 'Forefather' is recommended as a replacement.; [minor] Four events for a person mentioned only in a single verse of a genealogy are excessive. The last three events largely overlap and actually concern the theological significance of the genealogy in general, not Addi specifically. It is recommended to reduce this to two events.; [minor] The summary is good, but the expression 'Messiah's lineage' is somewhat archaic. A small linguistic improvement can be made.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. At least one footnote should be added about the meaning of the name, the differences between Luke's and Matthew's genealogies, or similar topics.

versions.title: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 in wording and structure ('Addi is a person mentioned in Jesus' genealogy in the Gospel of Luke. He is the son of Kosam and father of Melki,...'). It should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from the previous version.; [minor] The second key event ('Part of Nathan's lineage') is more of a theological observation than an event Addi participated in. Nevertheless, this is acceptable given that we have no other information, but the description could be tightened.; [minor] The era 'return' (the return from exile) is a reasonable placement for Addi, but it is uncertain exactly when he lived. Luke's genealogy provides limited chronological information for this period. The era can be accepted as a qualified estimate.

versions.summary: Addi appears in the genealogy that Luke gives for Jesus, where he is placed between his father Kosam and his son Melki. He belongs to the branch of King David's descendants that goes through Nathan, not through Solomon as Matthew's genealogy shows. Although the Bible tells us nothing about Addi's life or deeds, his place in the messianic line has theological significance: it shows how God faithfully carried forward the promise-line from David through generation after generation, all the way to Jesus Christ.
versions.title: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
versions.reason: [minor] The second key event element ('Part of Nathan's lineage') is actually not a separate event, but a theological observation linked to the same verse (Luke 3:28). Verses 28–31 are included to show broader context, but it gives the impression that Addi himself plays a role in an event beyond just being listed in the genealogy. This is fine as additional information, but could have been phrased more clearly as theological contextualization rather than an event.; [minor] Era 'return' (the return from exile) is a reasonable placement based on the fact that Addi is located between David and Jesus in Luke's genealogy. Exact dating is impossible, but the placement is defensible given the order in the genealogy.; [minor] The footnote's reference to '1 Chronicles 6:41' for the Levite Adaja may vary depending on different verse numbering systems in 1 Chronicles 6 (Hebrew vs. Greek numbering). It may be worth double-checking this reference, but it is not incorrect in itself.

footnotes.text: The name Addi (Greek: Ἀδδί) may be an abbreviated form of the Hebrew Adaja, meaning "the Lord's adornment" or "whom the Lord has adorned." Several individuals named Adaja appear in the Old Testament, including a Levite in 1 Chronicles 6:41 and the father of King Josiah's mother in 2 Kings 22:1.

Luke's genealogy follows the line of David's son Nathan, while Matthew follows the line of Solomon. This difference has been the subject of much theological discussion throughout church history. A common explanation is that Luke presents Mary's biological lineage, whereas Matthew presents Joseph's legal lineage, though other interpretations also exist.

Many of the names in Luke's genealogy between David and Zerubbabel do not appear in other biblical sources. This suggests that Luke may have had access to family records otherwise lost. Jewish families placed great emphasis on preserving such records, especially within priestly and royal lines, and this practice continued into the Second Temple period.

In rabbinic tradition, genealogical records were considered vital for establishing a person's tribal affiliation and rights. After the return from the Babylonian exile, such records were used to verify priestly and Levitical descent (cf. Ezra 2:62), highlighting the cultural context in which Luke's genealogy was composed.

The Greek form Ἀδδί likely corresponds to the Hebrew עַדִּי (Addi), which can be understood as "my adornment" or "my jewel." The suffix -i may be a possessive ending (first person singular), giving the name a personal character: "my ornament [is the Lord]" – a common type of theophoric short form in Semitic naming traditions.
